source.title: Structure and Scale in Simplicial Sequence Modelling

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in a synthetic sequence-prediction setting and reports that representation-error scaling becomes non-monotonic at long training times, qualifying the idea of a single smooth power law.
record.gate_note: The study varies training steps while keeping the architecture and parameter count fixed; fresh training sequences are generated for each batch, so steps, compute, and unique sequences scale together. It does not test parameter-count scaling, a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or the cited scaling-law results. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study reports held-out excess cross-entropy of small transformers on synthetic HMM sequences as training steps grow, with compute and fresh data scaling together at fixed size. This is a new-setting result on the power-law form (V5). It does not argue that a version is wrong, so T3 fits better than T5. The long-run non-monotonicity concerns probe error, not loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that scaling in prediction loss correlates with smooth but non-monotonic refinement of linearly encoded belief representations. They claim only smooth, roughly power-law improvement for the first ≈30M steps, they do not establish causation, and they say the trends may have multiple regimes.
record.recipe_differences: A fixed-size transformer on synthetic HMM sequences is scaled by training steps; parameters are not swept, and compute and fresh data scale together.
record.method_sensitivity: The long-run probe-loss curve differs from the earlier trend: it becomes non-monotonic and apparently begins to plateau. The 100-million-step result is from one transformer.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear-probe error in reconstructing Bayesian beliefs falls roughly as a power law up to 10M steps. In one 100M-step run it then dips non-monotonically and begins to plateau, a pattern the authors explain with a toy model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal representation error scales roughly as a power law with training before departing from it and approaching a nonzero plateau.

record.code_released: https://github.com/matomatical/hijax (cited as the source of a JAX training implementation from which this implementation was derived)
record.problems: The models are small and trained on a synthetic sequence task with fixed architecture. The prediction-loss run reaches 10 million steps, while the 100-million-step observation concerns probe loss from one transformer. The authors call for more careful analysis of the power-law trends; no uncertainty estimates are stated.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss. No parameter or token sweeps at text scale.
No extrapolation from fitted small runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
No image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. No parameter scaling: only steps, with compute and data tied together. No fitted exponent.
No comparison of parameter counting, schedules, fitting methods or data choices. No fit is performed.

missing.what: Authors state that both the performance and representation trends seem to have multiple regimes with different exponents, and that a careful power-law analysis is still needed.
Excess prediction loss occasionally goes negative (out-predicting Bayes on the fixed eval batch) and then returns positive, which limits how far the loss curve can be read near the floor.

record.verdict_notes: The setting is tiny and synthetic, and only training steps are scaled, with compute and data tied together. Evidence for V5 is weak and qualitative. The reader's V7 label wrongly relied on R3, which measures probe error; the V7 verdict here rests on the authors' text instead. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model pretraining loss, and scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute while the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No fits on small runs are used to predict larger-run losses.
Architecture is fixed; depth, width, or other architecture details are not compared.
No image or video models, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer. The tested setting is synthetic HMM sequence prediction.
The study does not compare parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods, data choices, or compute-optimal splits across setups.

rows.subject: 16 transformers (mean)
rows.operation_detail: Varied training steps with architecture fixed; compute and fresh training sequences scaled linearly with steps.

conditions.value: four residual blocks; one attention head of width 8 and one MLP layer of width 256
mess3 HMM sequences; fresh sequences for each batch

rows.measure: Held-out next-token cross-entropy minus Bayes-optimal cross-entropy on a fixed batch of 1024 sequences
rows.baseline: Per-seed Bayes-optimal cross-entropy on the held-out batch, subtracted to obtain excess prediction loss
rows.value: The excess prediction loss continually improves with compute, roughly as a power law.
rows.note: The plotted mean is for 16 seeds; the text characterizes the trend as roughly power-law-shaped for approximately the first 30 million steps.
rows.check: The note says the trend is roughly power-law for about 30 million steps, but the prediction-loss runs stop at 10 million steps. The 30-million figure is the authors' overall caveat. No exponent or fit is reported; the trend is described only as 'roughly as a power law'. Appendix A adds that excess loss sometimes dips below zero near the Bayes floor.

rows.subject: 16 transformers (mean)
rows.operation_detail: Measured linear-probe reconstruction error as training steps increased.

conditions.value: four residual blocks; one attention head of width 8 and one MLP layer of width 256

rows.measure: Mean squared error reconstructing Bayesian belief distributions from final-layer activations
rows.value: Probe loss quickly enters a regime of continual improvement, roughly as a power law.
rows.note: This is representation error, not held-out prediction cross-entropy, so it does not directly measure the loss behavior named in the claim versions.
rows.check: Linear-probe representation error is not a loss measure named by any version. The link to none is correct.

rows.subject: one transformer
rows.operation_detail: Measured linear-probe reconstruction error during a 100-million-step training run.
rows.measure: Mean squared error reconstructing Bayesian belief distributions from final-layer activations
rows.value: Between 10 million and 100 million steps, probe loss is non-monotonic: it turns around and then apparently begins to plateau.
rows.note: This concerns representation error rather than the held-out cross-entropy loss in the claim.
rows.check: This is probe error from a single 100M-step run, not prediction loss, so it should not support a V7 verdict. The V7 label's link to R3 is wrong.

relationships.condition: Synthetic mess3 HMM sequence prediction, 142K-parameter transformer, mean of 16 seeds, up to 10M training steps
relationships.reason: Held-out excess cross-entropy falls continually and roughly as a power law in steps (compute and data) (R1). This is a qualitative description with no fitted exponent.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out excess cross-entropy decreased continually and approximately as a power law in training steps, without a fitted exponent.

relationships.condition: Same synthetic setting; authors' qualitative reading of the loss and probe-error curves
relationships.reason: Text-based (Section 4; no row records it): the authors say any power laws 'appear to have multiple regimes with different exponents', which points to curves bending away from a single power law. No fit is reported.
relationships.display_finding: The authors described loss and probe-error curves as appearing to contain multiple regimes with different exponents, without reporting fitted laws.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic mess3 sequence prediction, up to approximately 30 million training steps
reader_labels.reason: The mean held-out excess prediction loss improves roughly as a power law in this synthetic sequence-modeling setting (R1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The authors restrict their power-law characterization to the first approximately 30 million steps and say more careful analysis is needed; the long-run non-monotonic result is for representation error, not prediction loss (R1, R3).
